meta.title: Who really said "You wouldn't worry so much about what other people think of you if you realized how seldom they do"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Eleanor Roosevelt never said it. Quote Investigator traces this line to humorist Olin Miller in December 1936; the Roosevelt credit is a later, unsourced graft.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You wouldn't worry so much about what other people think of you if you realized how seldom they do'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Eleanor Roosevelt. The earliest documented version (Dec. 1936) is credited to humorist Olin Miller; the Roosevelt attribution is spurious.

answer.label: Not Eleanor Roosevelt — traced to humorist Olin Miller
answer.sourceLine: There is no record of Eleanor Roosevelt writing or saying this. Quote Investigator ↗ found the earliest strong match in December 1936, credited to the humorist Olin Miller, and concludes he is the most likely originator; the wording popularly pinned on Roosevelt is a later, smoothed variant of Miller’s line. QI calls the Roosevelt attribution “spurious.”

source.rightsNote: The thought is traceable to a 1936 newspaper aphorism credited to Olin Miller, but the exact Roosevelt-attributed wording is an unsourced later paraphrase with no identifiable published origin, so no clean copyright status can be asserted. Because we cannot tie this precise wording to a specific work or edition, we mark rights “uncertain.”

author.name: Olin Miller
author.heading: About Olin Miller
author.bio: Olin Miller was an American humorist and syndicated newspaper columnist active from the 1930s. Quote Investigator identifies him as the most likely originator of this saying, citing a December 1936 newspaper item and follow-on appearances crediting him in Walter Winchell’s column (1937) and Reader’s Digest (1939). He is little remembered today, which is part of why the aphorism drifted onto more famous names.

misattribution.heading: How it landed on Eleanor Roosevelt
misattribution.intro: This is a classic case of a homeless aphorism drifting onto a magnet name. The line is older than its famous credits, and Eleanor Roosevelt is one of several people who acquired it decades after it first appeared.

items.why: Widely shared as Roosevelt’s, but Quote Investigator ↗ found no original source and calls the connection “spurious”; it is absent from her sourced record on Wikiquote ↗.
Sometimes attached to Twain as well — another default magnet for orphaned witticisms — with no supporting source, per Quote Investigator ↗.
A reworded version (“you’ll stop worrying what others think about you when you realize how seldom they do”) circulates under Wallace, who used the idea long after 1936 rather than coining it.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented form dates to December 1936 and is credited to humorist Olin Miller, per Quote Investigator ↗ — not Eleanor Roosevelt.

context.heading: Why the attribution sticks
lead: The saying is emotionally useful — a tidy reassurance for social anxiety — and that is exactly the kind of line that gets reassigned to a beloved authority figure. Eleanor Roosevelt, remembered for warmth and moral steadiness, is a natural host, so the quote reads as “something she would say” even though the paper trail runs to an obscure humorist.

Quote Investigator’s trail — Olin Miller in 1936, Walter Winchell in 1937, Reader’s Digest in 1939 — predates any Roosevelt credit by decades, which is the tell: the words were already in wide circulation before her name was attached.
context.pull: Older than its famous credits — the mark of a drifting aphorism.
